text:
Marathon Petroleum jumped 2.8% over the last two trading days, capping a sharp reversal from last week's decline. The move tracks a significant widening between U.S. and world oil prices — the gap has grown to $17.80 per barrel (U.S. at $96.16, world at $113.96) — reflecting supply disruptions in the Middle East from tanker strikes and the Strait of Hormuz tensions. For a U.S. refiner like Marathon, this gap is valuable: it can buy cheaper domestic crude and sell refined products into a tighter global market, improving margins. Refineries are running at 92.5% capacity, near practical maximums, so the company can capture this advantage at high utilization.

The broader backdrop is acute: geopolitical risk in the Middle East is pushing world prices higher while the U.S. sits on ample domestic supplies (over 711 million barrels in storage). Although the G7's plan to release diesel stocks could eventually pressure prices, the immediate dynamic—Iran rhetoric, tanker strikes, and naval buildup—keeps the global-to-domestic spread wide enough to support refinery economics.
